results.title: temperature2 ships /gpu/: what compute actually costs
highlights:
TL;DR 

- ▸ An H100 SXM hour settled at $2.68 on 26 August 2026, a B200 hour at $6.22 and an RTX 5090 hour at $0.54 — 92 days of daily settlements, all charted.
- ▸ Token prices fell far harder than rent this month: OpenAI's blended price is down 68.0% over 31 days while H100 rent moved -1.5%.
- ▸ The board carries volatility, rebased depreciation curves, generational ratios and $/PFLOP-hour, all computed here from the published series with the method written next to each number.
- ▸ One GPU-hour has to produce 1.83M tokens to cover its own rent at Anthropic's blended price and 26.15M at DeepSeek's — a 14.28x spread in what a token is worth.
- ▸ Prices are from the Ornn Data public index; the public window is rolling, so the site keeps its own archive and never rewrites a recorded day.

...

## The board

Five GPUs, one row each, 92 days of daily settlements from 27 May to 26 August 2026.

| GPU | USD/hour | 92d | Volatility | Range | $/PFLOP-hr |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B200 | $6.22 | +17.1% | 60% | $4.22 – $7.28 | $2.76 |
| H200 | $4.24 | +8.7% | 97% | $2.99 – $5.62 | $4.29 |
| H100 SXM | $2.68 | -2.9% | 63% | $2.29 – $3.17 | $2.71 |
| A100 SXM4 | $1.06 | -14.5% | 39% | $0.99 – $1.31 | $3.40 |
| RTX 5090 | $0.54 | -37.2% | 74% | $0.48 – $1.33 | $2.58 |

Prices settled 26 August 2026, Ornn Data Compute Price Index. Volatility is the annualized standard deviation of daily log returns scaled by the square root of 365 — calendar days rather than trading days, because compute rents on weekends and a 252-day scaling would understate it by about 17%. That measure, the changes, the ranges and the per-unit columns are all computed on this site from the published daily series, not read from a paid analytics endpoint, which is why the method can be stated instead of cited.

...

## How fast old silicon gets cheap

`/gpu/#decay` rebases all five series to 100 on 27 May, which is the only honest way to put a $6.22 hour and a $0.54 hour on one axis. Absolute dollars hide the slope, and the slope is the story.

Over the window the RTX 5090 fell 37.2% and the A100 SXM4 fell 14.5%, while the B200 rose 17.1% and the H200 rose 8.7%. Nothing wore out. The hardware behind the falling lines performs exactly as it did in May; what changed is that supply caught up and newer parts pulled demand off the older ones. A rental series is not an accounting schedule, but it is the market’s live opinion about the same question a depreciation schedule answers on a spreadsheet, and it updates every day rather than every quarter.

...

## What a GPU-hour has to produce

Rent divided by token price. Millions of tokens one GPU-hour must serve to cover its own rent, at each lab’s blended price on 26 August 2026:

| GPU | Anthropic | OpenAI | Google | DeepSeek |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| B200 | 4.25M | 15.62M | 20.94M | 60.68M |
| H200 | 2.90M | 10.65M | 14.28M | 41.37M |
| H100 SXM | 1.83M | 6.73M | 9.02M | 26.15M |
| A100 SXM4 | 0.72M | 2.66M | 3.57M | 10.34M |
| RTX 5090 | 0.37M | 1.36M | 1.82M | 5.27M |

The full table lives at `/gpu/#breakeven`. It is two published indices divided by each other and nothing else — it ignores the model being served, batch size, utilization, the lab’s own hardware deals, and every cost that is not the GPU. It answers exactly one question: how much output has to leave the card before the card has paid for itself. The 14.28x spread between the dearest and cheapest blended token price is the same 14.28x spread in how much work a rented hour has to do.

...

...

Rent is a market price, not a depreciation schedule. It moves when supply lands, when a newer part pulls demand off an older one, and when a large buyer takes capacity off the market. Over the 92 days to 26 August 2026 the RTX 5090 moved -37.2% and the A100 SXM4 -14.5%, while the B200 rose 17.1%. The silicon works exactly as well as it did in May.

results.title: The "AI Infrastructure" Trade Is Actually Two Trades: GPU Rentals and Power Tolls | AInvest
highlights:
- - Power landlords TeraWulf WULF-- and Cipher CIFR-- ($19B+ Anthropic/Google contracts) trade below backlog value, earning per megawatt while avoiding GPU depreciation risks.

- - Meta's $27B+ self-built "Meta Compute" triggered 14-17% drops in GPU renters, exposing fragility when clients become competitors.

- - The sector now splits into 44x P/S GPU renters vs. undervalued power hosts, with outcomes hinging on contract renewals and construction timelines.

...

The weakness hiding inside the metric: backlog is a promise to pay, and the promises are concentrated in a handful of whales. OpenAI alone is roughly a third of CoreWeave's business. And the more skeptical analysts in the space note that part of this "demand" is a financing loop — customers and chipmakers helping fund the very fleets that then owe them years of revenue.

...

The power landlords: paid per megawatt, not per GPU-hour.

TeraWulf and Cipher took the other path, one that two years ago looked like the uninspiring side of the sector. They were bitcoin BTC-- miners — land, substations, cheap wattage, no reputation to defend. Their pivot to AI is real, but it's structurally different: they don't buy the chips. They sign ten-year leases to wrap buildings, power, and cooling around someone else's GPUs, and they charge per megawatt whether the machines inside make money or not. The tenant owns the depreciation.

The contract terms show why this matters. TeraWulf's 200-megawatt hosting agreement with Fluidstack is worth about $3.7 billion over ten years, with more if extended, and Google backstops $1.8 billion of its tenant's obligations; TeraWulf has since signed a $19 billion lease with Anthropic for capacity at its Kentucky campus. Cipher carries roughly $11.4 billion of contracted hosting backlog — against a stock-market value of about $7 billion — including a 168-megawatt Fluidstack deal that Google backstops to the tune of $1.4 billion. This is what analysts mean when they say the miner-hosters trade below their contract value: the market is pricing these leases as if a large share will never turn into cash.

The catch is timing. The tenants show up later than the hype. Cipher's second quarter brought in only about $25 million of revenue and a $267.5 million net loss, most of it a non-cash warrant charge, as bitcoin revenue drains away faster than the AI leases ramp. TeraWulf is further along — $31.9 million of HPC lease revenue in Q2, about 71% of total revenue — but still loss-making.

The landlords don't own chip risk; they own the risk that power arrives on schedule and tenants keep paying.

...

On July 1, Bloomberg reported that Meta — the whale that had already committed roughly $27 billion to Nebius and $21 billion to CoreWeave — was building "Meta Compute" to sell raw capacity and hosted models to outsiders. CoreWeave fell about 14% and Nebius about 17% in a single session; Meta's own shares rose on the news. The selloff kept going through mid-July as efficiency scares — a Kimi K3 generation of models rerunning the DeepSeek playbook — hit the sector.

The rush to call it "overcapacity" was wrong in one important sense. SemiAnalysis, the industry's sharpest independent engineering voice, pointed out that Meta's own procurement is not slowing: it contracted more than five gigawatts of capacity in the first half of 2026 alone, and its 2027 capital spending will be "astonishingly high". A buyer that sells its surplus is a buyer that values compute more than the price it can extract. Demand was never the problem.

But the sell-off exposed the right thing. For the GPU owners, a rental backlog is only as solid as the whale paying it, and the whales are the very companies building the most in-house supply. When your single biggest customer announces itself as a potential competitor, the "backlog is guaranteed revenue" math stops holding even if no contract is broken. The landlords were barely touched by the same scare — their revenue is anchored to power and construction, not to whoever holds the marginal GPU.

...

None of it is settled by Nvidia's $96 billion in revenue. Nvidia collects a 75% gross margin whether the intermediaries' whales renew or not; its economics don't depend on the answer. The GPU owners' profits depend on utilization, on the terms at the end of those three-to-five-year contracts, and on refinancing — CoreWeave's newest $2.6 billion facility runs five years, longer than the roughly three-year average of its own customer contracts, a bet by lenders that GPU demand outlasts the contracts meant to service the debt. The landlords' profits depend on construction timetables and tenant credit.

That's why the two halves now trade where they do: Nebius at roughly 44x trailing sales, CoreWeave around 20x trailing EBITDA — the market paying for years of booked backlog as if it were already cash — while Cipher trades at a fraction of its contracted backlog, the market doubting the leases will convert. Both can't be fully right, and neither discount is certain; the renewals and the construction schedules will identify which was wrong.

results.title: GPU Rental Price Index — H100, H200, B200 & A100 $/Hour | ComputingPower.org
highlights:
A GPU rental price index answers one question: what does an hour of a given accelerator cost right now, across the market, rather than at one provider? This page condenses the same dataset that powers the live pricing table on the homepage into a low / median / high figure per GPU, explains how the index is built, and shows how to read the other published GPU price indices you will run into.

$2.29 Lowest H100 80GB / hr

$3.58 Lowest H200 141GB / hr

$5.89 Lowest B200 192GB / hr

$1.65 Lowest A100 80GB / hr

## The index: on-demand $/GPU-hour by accelerator

Each row summarises the public on-demand rate for one GPU (or one GPU inside a multi-GPU node, expressed per GPU) across every provider in the dataset that lists it. "Median" is the middle listing — a better benchmark than the minimum, which is often a single marketplace host in one region.

| Accelerator | Listings | Low $/hr | Median $/hr | High $/hr | Cheapest in dataset | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| NVIDIA B200 192GB | 5 | $5.89 | $6.89 | $7.99 | Crusoe | Blackwell; supply still tight, mostly reservation-first |
| NVIDIA H200 141GB | 9 | $3.58 | $4.95 | $10.60 | Crusoe | Hyperscaler on-demand is 2–3× the specialist-cloud rate |
| NVIDIA H100 80GB | 14 | $2.29 | $2.97 | $4.99 | FluidStack | The most liquid SKU; the reference point for every index |
| AMD MI325X 256GB | 3 | $2.25 | $2.35 | $2.49 | Vast.ai | Priced against H100 on memory per dollar |
| AMD MI300X 192GB | 2 | $1.99 | $2.44 | $2.89 | FluidStack | Popular for large-model inference (192 GB on one card) |
| NVIDIA A100 80GB | 12 | $1.65 | $2.46 | $3.67 | FluidStack | See the cheapest A100 comparison |
| NVIDIA RTX 4090 24GB | 4 | $0.65 | $0.71 | $0.79 | FluidStack | Consumer card; marketplaces only, no NVLink |
| Google TPU v7 | 1 | $8.50 (Google Cloud only) | | | Google Cloud | Ironwood; per-chip, on-demand |
| Google TPU v6e | 1 | $3.22 (Google Cloud only) | | | Google Cloud | Trillium; see TPU explained |
| AWS Trainium3 / Trainium2 | 1 each | $3.85 / $2.15 (AWS only) | | | AWS | Per accelerator inside Trn instances |
| Intel Gaudi 3 / Gaudi 2 | 1 each | $1.99 / $1.29 (Intel Cloud) | | | Intel Tiber | Limited third-party availability |

Rates are public on-demand list prices in USD per GPU-hour recorded in the ComputingPower.org dataset; single-vendor accelerators have no spread. Spot, reserved and negotiated contract rates are lower — see the spread section below. Always confirm the current figure on the provider's pricing page before committing.

...

The on-demand rate is the ceiling, not the market. For the H100 the same dataset implies roughly this ladder:

| H100 80GB pricing tier | Typical $/GPU-hr | Relative to on-demand median |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hyperscaler on-demand | $4.99 | +68% |
| Specialist-cloud on-demand (index median) | $2.97 | — |
| Marketplace / cheapest on-demand | $2.29 | −23% |
| 1-year committed / reserved | ≈ $2.00–2.40 | −20% to −35% |
| Spot / interruptible | ≈ $1.00–1.80 | −40% to −65% |
| Multi-year negotiated cluster contract | below public rates | not published |

...

Reading the trend: H100 on-demand rates fell from the $8–9/hr seen at the 2023 shortage peak to the ~$2–3/hr range as supply caught up and H200/B200 arrived. Each new generation tends to push the previous one's price down rather than raising the overall $/GPU-hour, so an index expressed in $/hour understates the fall in cost per unit of compute.

results.title: Amazon Just Committed to 2 Million More Nvidia GPUs, and the Stock Traded Lower | The Motley Fool
highlights:
- AWS will deploy 2 million additional Nvidia GPUs in 2027 and 2028, on top of the more than 1 million it committed to earlier this year.
- Amazon raised its 2026 capital spending estimate from about $200 billion to about $220 billion in July.
- AWS revenue grew 37% year over year in the second quarter, the segment's fastest growth since 2021.

Amazon (AMZN -0.29%) got the kind of news on Wednesday that artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure stocks usually rally on. Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Nvidia (NVDA -2.01%) announced that AWS will deploy 2 million additional Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs) across its global infrastructure in 2027 and 2028. The commitment roughly triples the total the cloud giant had signed up for just five months earlier.

...

Which is it for Amazon shareholders: confirmation that demand for AI computing keeps outrunning supply, or 2 million more reasons to worry about a capital budget that already reached $220 billion this year?

...

At Nvidia's GTC conference in March, AWS announced plans to add more than 1 million Nvidia GPUs starting in 2026. Since then, demand has exceeded those expectations, the companies said Wednesday. AWS now plans to deploy an additional 2 million GPUs (Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra, Rubin, and Rubin Ultra chips) in 2027 and 2028. That takes the committed total from more than 1 million to more than 3 million.

...

Amazon's capital spending was climbing before any of this. In February, the company estimated 2026 capital expenditures of about $200 billion, and it held that estimate in April. Then, on July's earnings call, CEO Andy Jassy raised the figure to about $220 billion, citing the higher cost of memory.

The money is already being spent. Amazon's purchases of property and equipment, net of what it gets back from sales and incentives, totaled $169 billion over the trailing 12 months as of the second quarter of 2026 -- an increase of $66.1 billion year over year that the company ties primarily to its investments in AI. Operating cash flow rose 33% to $161.4 billion over the same stretch. And free cash flow swung to an outflow of $7.6 billion, down from an inflow of $18.2 billion a year earlier.

"Even at that amount, we will still not have enough capacity to meet all the demand we have in 2026, and I believe this dynamic will also be true in 2027, too," Jassy said on the call. "In fact, the demand we already have for 2028 is striking."

That timing matters here. The new GPUs arrive in 2027 and 2028, past the window this year's budget covers. In other words, Wednesday's commitment signals that spending stays elevated well beyond 2026.

results.title: Interpretation of the JPMorgan research report: AI token spending increased by 7% month-on-month, B200 leasing declined for the first time, DRAM prices have risen for five consecutive months.
highlights:
The demand signals for AI infrastructure are diverging. Spending on large model tokens continues to grow, while B200 GPU leasing prices have seen their first decline in over six months, and DRAM spot prices have increased for the fifth consecutive month.

...

## GPU leasing prices diverge: B200 declines for the first time, H100 rebounds

The GPU leasing market is experiencing structural price differentiation.

A100 leasing prices remained stable at $1.65 per GPU hour in August. H100 rebounded to $2.73, an increase of 1.2% month-on-month. B200 dropped by 1.5% to $5.63, marking the first month-on-month decline since the B200 index was released in September 2025. The price ratio between B200 and H100 decreased from 2.12 times to 2.06 times, while the price ratio between H100 and A100 increased from 1.64 times to 1.65 times.

The weakening price of B200 reflects that the supply of the next generation of GPUs is ramping up. Over the past six months, B200 prices have consistently risen due to supply shortages, but recent capacity increases are marginally easing the tension. The rebound in H100 prices indicates that demand for the previous generation of products remains resilient, and prices have not been entirely squeezed out of the market.

...

JPMorgan's data points to a diverging AI infrastructure market. Token spending is growing while prices are compressed, GPU leasing is experiencing generational differentiation, and storage prices are generally strong. The fundamentals of demand have not loosened, and structural changes on the supply side, including new capacity releases and the popularity of low-priced models, are reshaping pricing logic. For equipment suppliers, the price signals of DRAM and NAND still constitute positive support; for the GPU leasing market, the first price drop of B200 may just be the beginning.

results.title: IREN ARR hits $4bn with 2026 capacity sold out - UK Investor Magazine
highlights:
IREN shares fell in US trade as investors weighed rising ARR against the capex required for future revenues to be achieved. 

The Nasdaq-listed group said revenue from its AI Cloud Services business grew roughly eightfold to $128.8m in the year to 30 June, and that it now has $4bn of contracted annualised run-rate revenue tied to its 2026 capacity, of which around $1bn is operating today. 

In addition, it said it had signed a new multi-year AI cloud contract with a leading frontier AI lab, as the company accelerates its pivot from Bitcoin mining to renting out data centre capacity for artificial intelligence.

Its capacity for 2026 is largely sold out, with a customer base that includes Cohere, Perplexity and Figure AI alongside the newly signed frontier lab.

IREN was once a bitcoin miner and reported a net loss for the year, driven by around $639m of non-cash impairments as it decommissions Bitcoin mining hardware and converts sites to support AI. Adjusted earnings also softened in the final quarter, reflecting higher staff costs and broader platform investment ahead of the ramp-up in AI revenue.

To fund the build-out, IREN has leaned heavily on financing. It secured $3.6bn of investment-grade GPU financing at 6% to support a contract with Microso and lined up a further $2.8bn for other deployments, including a $2.4bn facility led by Blue Owl and PIMCO.

...

“We started IREN with a simple observation: the digital world can scale almost instantly, but the physical world cannot,” said Daniel Roberts, Co-Founder and Co-CEO of IREN. 

“This year, that founding thesis became tangible. Exponential AI consumption growth has fueled demand for compute capacity well beyond the available supply of infrastructure. IREN was built for this moment. Our 2026 capacity is largely sold out. This includes Horizon 1, the first of four leading-edge liquid cooled GPU deployments that we successfully delivered to Microsoft this month. We have broadened our customer base to include hyperscalers, enterprises, AI developers and frontier labs. As our platform has scaled and our market position has strengthened, we have attracted leading customers and secured stronger pricing, more attractive contract terms and improved paybacks.”

results.title: Anthropic dropped a $7B bid for chip startup MatX
highlights:
The timing puts this in the middle of a broader scramble among AI labs to stop renting all their compute from Nvidia. OpenAI’s first in-house chip, Jalapeño, already claims better inference throughput than Nvidia’s Blackwell on OpenAI’s own workloads, as we covered on 2026-08-26. Anthropic itself has been working both sides of the compute problem at once: it just committed $45 billion to Nscale for 460 megawatts of Nvidia Vera Rubin capacity, reported here yesterday, while separately meeting with “a range of AI chip startups,” per Reuters, as it tries to figure out whether to build, buy, or rent its way to custom silicon. An abandoned $7 billion acquisition suggests Anthropic decided buying MatX outright wasn’t the right shape for that bet, at least not yet.

The economics explain the urgency even without a specific number attached to Anthropic’s internal chip roadmap. Renting an Nvidia H100 cost $2.68 per GPU-hour as of 2026-08-26, down 8.5% in a week, according to Ornn Data’s Compute Price Index (charted at /gpu/), and H200 pricing fell almost 20% over the same 30 days. Prices moving that fast in either direction is exactly the kind of volatility a lab the size of Anthropic wants insulation from, and owning or co-designing chips is the classic hedge, the same logic that pushed Google to TPUs and Amazon to Trainium years ago. A $7 billion all-cash purchase of a chip startup is a much bigger, much more permanent bet than a compute lease, and pulling back from it while still shopping other chip startups reads as Anthropic deciding it wants the option without the commitment.

results.title: Nvidia Price Hike Triggers ASIC Pivot as GPU Cloud Margins Crack · Slicast
highlights:
Nvidia's $96 billion quarter and 15% price hike cement its pricing dominance, but this margin extraction is accelerating hyperscaler migration to custom ASICs like OpenAI's Jalapeño and exposing critical refinancing vulnerabilities for GPU-cloud operators as capex scales beyond sustainable returns.

Nvidia delivered $96.2 billion in Q2 revenue, up 106% year-over-year, driven by a Vera Rubin ramp that projects $20 billion in sales for Q3 alone—marking its fastest historical velocity and capturing 20% of data center revenue immediately. This momentum is backed by a strategic lever pull: Nvidia has notified cloud providers of a 15% price increase effective in 2027, citing escalating packaging and component costs. Microsoft's signaled $678 billion capex commitment confirms hyperscalers are absorbing this inflation to secure capacity, yet the price adjustment fundamentally alters the ROI calculus for the entire supply chain, shifting surplus value decisively back to the silicon vendor.

...

GPU-cloud intermediaries face acute financial exposure as Nvidia's cost pass-through collides with fixed-capacity leases. Riot Platforms secured a $9.1 billion compute lease with Anthropic, but its financing bridge loan matures before rental payments begin, highlighting a dangerous refinancing gap for mining-to-AI pivots dependent on long-term off-take agreements. Similarly, Nscale's $45 billion six-year contract with Anthropic anchors revenue visibility but locks in massive capital requirements for the Monarch Compute Campus, exposing tenants to execution and power-delivery risks. As Nvidia extracts more value per rack, the spread between wholesale GPU-cloud pricing and underlying hardware costs narrows, turning infrastructure leasing into a high-risk capital game rather than a scalable arbitrage play.
